verdict: Lend selectively to Mumbai commercial real estate: pursue leased-up office and retail owners with rental cover and completed approvals; avoid under-construction redevelopment and slum/tenancy-heavy projects until approvals and possession are documented.
title: Mumbai Commercial Real Estate: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
Commercial real estate in Mumbai turns land, approvals and construction capital into rent or sale proceeds. **Cash sits in two places: rent rolls on completed assets, and inventory (sold or unsold) on under-construction ones.** The cycle is long: land and approvals first, construction next, then lease-up or sell-out. Pricing power exists only where the asset is completed, leased and in a scarce micro-market; elsewhere the developer is a price-taker. Capex is front-loaded and funded by debt, so the lender is effectively financing approvals and construction before a rupee of rent arrives.

## What has changed now
Local news is mixed and thin on this city's credit data. **A large Mumbai mixed-use asset changed hands: Marathon Nextgen is buying Adani Group's 60 per cent stake in a Mumbai project for Rs 335 crore [1].** Separately, MHADA issued a stop-work notice on the Mahavir Compound redevelopment at Matunga, with 95 shop owners awaiting possession [2]. A Marathi report flags developer stress in Navi Mumbai [3]. Peer results are stronger: Brigade reported a 29% year-on-year rise in average realisation to Rs 13,841 per square foot [5], and Phoenix Mills' office income rose 64% on higher occupancy across Mumbai and Pune assets [7]. Rating commentary on Mindspace REIT notes refinancing risk from bullet CP/NCD maturities, partly offset by cash and undrawn facilities [9][11]. Treat the peer and rating items as context, not Mumbai-specific proof.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue owners of completed, leased-up office and retail assets in Mumbai with rental cash flow covering debt.** Phoenix's office income surge on occupancy [7] and Brigade's realisation gains [5] show where pricing power sits. Also pursue acquirers taking full control of mixed-use assets, as in the Rs 335 crore stake purchase [1], provided they fund it with equity and disclosed debt. **Avoid pure redevelopment and tenancy-heavy projects until approvals and possession are clean**; the Matunga stop-work notice [2] is exactly the approval risk that stalls cash flow.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against rent, not against hope.** For leased assets, take assignment of receivables, a debt-service cover covenant and a cash sweep. For under-construction, tie disbursement to approvals and construction milestones. Every month take: rent roll and occupancy, collections vs billing, approval status, and debt maturity profile. **Ask for the refinancing plan wherever bullet CP/NCD maturities exist [9][11].** Where a figure is missing, collect from customer.

## Early-warning signs
- Occupancy or rent collections falling month-on-month -> freeze fresh disbursement and re-price. - Stop-work or approval notices, as at Matunga [2] -> halt drawdown until cleared. - Bullet maturities approaching without refinancing lined up [9] -> require a refinance term sheet. - Stake-sale or equity infusion at a discount to book [1] -> reassess collateral value.
watch: Occupancy falls or collections slip -> freeze disbursement and review pricing
Any stop-work or approval lapse -> halt drawdown until cleared
Sale at discount to book -> reassess collateral and covenant
Cover falls below covenant -> escalate and seek cash sweep
